claim: After 24 hours of starvation, both male and female Drosophila melanogaster flies preferred a sugar diet supplemented with autolyzed yeast over a diet composed exclusively of sugar.
source: Using a new real-time feeding monitoring system called FLIC, which quantifies all contact interactions an individual fly has with food (Ro et al., 2014; http://www.wikiflic.com), we found that after mild starvation both male and female flies preferred a sugar diet supplemented with autolyzed yeast (the major protein source in the fly diet) over a diet composed exclusively of sugar (Figure 1A, 24 hr starvation).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from FLIC feeding monitoring system shown in Figure 1A, demonstrating preference behavior after 24hr starvation.

claim: Protein preference after starvation persisted for just over one day, with longer food deprivation increasing protein preference.
source: This preference persisted for just over one day, with longer food deprivation increasing protein preference (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by time-course data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing temporal dynamics and starvation duration effects.

claim: Fully-fed animals consumed a sugar-only diet more often throughout the experiment.
source: On the other hand, fully-fed animals consumed a sugar-only diet more often throughout the experiment (Figure 1A, fully-fed).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A for fully-fed condition.

claim: Food choice was not based on caloric content because starved flies chose a 1% protein diet over an isocaloric 1% sugar diet.
source: Food choice was not based on caloric content because starved flies also chose a 1% protein diet over an isocaloric 1% sugar diet and an increase in protein concentration to a hypercaloric 5% did not affect this preference (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing isocaloric diets shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Total feeding time was a much stronger predictor of total protein feeding time than it was of sugar feeding time.
source: Using this information we found that total feeding time was a much stronger predictor of total protein feeding time than it was of sugar feeding time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Flies with more total feeding time were more likely to choose a protein containing food as their first meal and to have a stronger protein preference over the course of the experiment.
source: Moreover, flies with more total feeding time were more likely to choose a protein containing food as their first meal and to have a stronger protein preference over the course of the experiment (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation between total feeding time and protein preference in Figure 1C.

claim: Following mild starvation, flies preferred autolyzed yeast to the same extent as a pure complex protein such as bovine serum albumin (BSA) over a wide range of concentrations.
source: Following mild starvation, flies preferred autolyzed yeast, which is primarily composed of short peptide/single amino acids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), to the same extent as a pure complex protein such as bovine serum albumin (BSA) (Figure 1D) over a wide range of concentrations, suggesting that behavioral preference for yeast is driven in whole or in part by its protein content.
evidence: Supported by dose-response data comparing autolyzed yeast and BSA preferences shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Twenty-four hour starvation had no detectable effect on internal protein levels.
source: Twenty-four hour starvation had no detectable effect on internal protein levels (Figure 1E), suggesting that preference was independent of gross protein stores.
evidence: Supported by metabolite quantification data shown in Figure 1E comparing fully-fed and 24hr-starved flies.

claim: Protein preference is not limited to reproductively active female flies and is more dynamic than previously suspected.
source: Protein preference is, therefore, not limited to reproductively active female flies (Ribeiro and Dickson, 2010; Vargas et al., 2010) and is more dynamic than previously suspected.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both males and females show protein preference after starvation, and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Disruption of serotonin signaling repeatedly reduced protein preference in starved flies.
source: Among all manipulations, disruption in serotonin signaling repeatedly reduced protein preference in starved flies (Figure 2A blue bars; Supplementary file 1 candidates 63, 65, 67, and 68).
evidence: Supported by candidate screen results shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Silencing of serotonergic neurons and treatment of flies with a serotonin receptor 2a (5HT2a) antagonist, ketanserin, eliminated protein preference entirely.
source: Silencing of serotonergic neurons and treatment of flies with a serotonin receptor 2a (5HT2a) antagonist, ketanserin (Colas et al., 1995), eliminated preference entirely, such that starved animals exhibited an aversion to dietary protein that mimicked what we routinely observed from fully-fed, control animals.
evidence: Supported by experimental manipulations described in the text and referenced in Figure 2A, with citation to ketanserin's specificity.

claim: Flies with significantly reduced tryptophan hydroxylase (Trh) exhibited a reduction in preference for both autolyzed yeast and BSA compared with control animals.
source: Flies with significantly reduced tryptophan hydroxylase (Trh), a rate-limiting enzyme for neuronal serotonin synthesis (Neckameyer et al., 2007) that is the Drosophila homologue of TPH2, exhibited a reduction in preference for both autolyzed yeast and BSA compared with control animals (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Trh mutants shown in Figure 2B,C and supplementary figures, with citation to Trh function.

claim: All of the 5HT2a manipulations abrogated the preference for protein following mild starvation.
source: We verified a role for 5HT2a by examining flies that carried two independent 5HT2a mutant alleles (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), flies transheterozygous for each allele (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), as well as flies with RNAi-mediated knock-down of 5HT2a transcript (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F). All of the 5HT2a manipulations abrogated the preference for protein following mild starvation, effectively recapitulating Trh mutation.
evidence: Supported by multiple genetic manipulations of 5HT2a shown in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: Loss of function in three other serotonin receptors (5HT1a, 5HT1b, and 5HT2b) had no effect on the preference phenotype.
source: Loss of function in three other serotonin receptors (5HT1a, 5HT1b, and 5HT2b; 5HT7 mutant animals were not viable) had no effect on the preference phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from other serotonin receptor mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Disruption of serotonin signaling did not disrupt other feeding preferences because Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies exhibited expected choice behaviors when presented with sweet vs bitter tastes or sweet vs sweeter food.
source: Disruption of serotonin signaling did not disrupt other feeding preferences because Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies exhibited expected choice behaviors when presented with sweet vs bitter tastes or sweet vs sweeter food (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B testing other taste preferences.

claim: When fully fed, the feeding behaviors of Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies are not different from control animals.
source: Furthermore, when fully fed, the feeding behaviors of Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies are not different from control animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing fully-fed mutant and control flies shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Flies retained their preference for dietary protein when serotonergic neurons were inactivated only during the starvation phase.
source: We found that flies retained their preference for dietary protein when serotonergic neurons were inactivated only during the starvation phase.
evidence: Supported by temporal manipulation experiments described in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Inactivation of serotonergic neurons only during the choice phase was sufficient to abolish preference and phenocopy the Trh mutant.
source: Inactivation only during the choice phase, however, was sufficient to abolish preference and phenocopy the Trh mutant, implying that serotonin may be involved specifically in protein reward after starvation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by temporal manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3A, with inference about serotonin's role in reward.

claim: Inhibition of serotonin signaling did not alter total food intake during the choice test.
source: Inhibition of serotonin signaling did not alter total food intake during the choice test, demonstrating that the lack of protein preference seen in transgenic flies is not an artifact of reduced feeding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Serotonin levels in the head were unchanged after starvation but increased 100–200% after flies consumed protein compared with the fully-fed condition.
source: Indeed, we observed that serotonin levels in the head were unchanged after starvation but increased 100–200% after flies consumed protein compared with the fully-fed condition (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by UPLC-MS measurements of serotonin shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was an acute increase in the abundance of 5HT2a mRNA, but not transcript from other serotonin receptors, in the heads of flies that were starved of all nutrients and refed with protein for 3 hr.
source: Much like the temporal profile of serotonin concentration, we observed an acute increase in the abundance of 5HT2a mRNA, but not transcript from other serotonin receptors, in the heads of flies that were starved of all nutrients and refed with protein for 3 hr (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements of serotonin receptor mRNA shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 5HT2a mRNA abundance was not affected by starvation alone, and it returned to the level of fully-fed animals after 24 hr of protein feeding.
source: 5HT2a mRNA abundance was not affected by starvation alone, and it returned to the level of fully-fed animals after 24 hr of protein feeding, which is coincident with their loss of feeding preference (e.g., Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 3C and correlation with behavioral data from Figure 1A.

claim: Activation of serotonergic neurons suppressed feeding in fully-fed flies.
source: Although activation of serotonergic neurons suppressed feeding as we expected (Gasque et al., 2013) (Figure 3D left), when fully-fed flies did eat, they showed a near absolute preference for protein-containing food (Figure 3D right; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dTrpA1 activation shown in Figure 3D, with citation to previous work on feeding suppression.

claim: When fully-fed flies with activated serotonergic neurons did eat, they showed a near absolute preference for protein-containing food.
source: Although activation of serotonergic neurons suppressed feeding as we expected (Gasque et al., 2013) (Figure 3D left), when fully-fed flies did eat, they showed a near absolute preference for protein-containing food (Figure 3D right; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dTrpA1 activation shown in Figure 3D right and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Serotonergic signaling increases the value of dietary protein in an energy-state dependent manner.
source: These results support the notion that serotonergic signaling increases the value of dietary protein in an energy-state dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the hyperactivation experiments showing that serotonin activation induces protein preference even in fully-fed flies.

claim: On a standard laboratory diet of low or intermediate yeast content, Trh mutants were long-lived, and loss of 5HT2a did not affect lifespan.
source: On a standard laboratory diet of low or intermediate yeast content, Trh mutants were long-lived, and loss of 5HT2a did not affect lifespan (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data on fixed diets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Trh mutant flies responded similarly to control animals when diet was manipulated in a traditional fixed-diet manner, while 5HT2a mutants showed a reduced response.
source: We found that Trh mutant flies responded similarly to control animals, while 5HT2a mutants showed a reduced response, when diet was manipulated in this traditional manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by diet manipulation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Control flies were shortest-lived in a sucrose-only diet.
source: As expected, control flies were shortest-lived in a sucrose-only diet (Lee et al., 2008; Skorupa et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data and citations to previous work on dietary effects on lifespan.

claim: Control animals in the choice environment lived substantially shorter than animals maintained in an isocaloric fixed diet or in one consisting of yeast-only.
source: On the other hand, we were surprised to observe that control animals in the choice environment lived substantially shorter than animals maintained in an isocaloric fixed diet or in one consisting of yeast-only (Figure 4A) despite exhibiting equivalent health metrics when young (e.g., Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data comparing different dietary conditions shown in Figure 4A and health metrics in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Trh mutant flies lived modestly longer than control flies on all control diets (Sucrose-only, Yeast-only, and Fixed diet), while 5HT2a mutants did not.
source: Consistent with our observations using standard protocols, Trh mutant flies lived modestly longer than control flies on all control diets (Figure 4A; Sucrose-only, Yeast-only, and Fixed diet), while 5HT2a mutants did not.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 4A comparing genotypes across different diets.

claim: When flies were aged in the choice environment, there was a near doubling (90% increase) of mean lifespan of both Trh and 5HT2a mutant animals.
source: However, when the flies were aged in the choice environment we observed a near doubling (90% increase) of mean lifespan of both Trh and 5HT2a mutant animals (Figure 4A, Choice diet).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data in the choice diet condition shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All flies consumed more food in the choice environment compared with an isocaloric fixed diet.
source: Using an indigestible dye mixed in both food wells we found that all flies consumed more food in the choice environment compared with an isocaloric fixed diet (Figure 4B, left two bar groups).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements using tracer dye shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Most of the increased consumption in the choice environment was due to a boost in sugar feeding.
source: By labeling foods in individual wells we found that most of that increased consumption was due to a boost in sugar feeding (Figure 4B, right two bar groups).
evidence: Supported by nutrient-specific food intake measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There were no differences among genotypes in total food consumption in any condition.
source: More importantly, we found no differences among genotypes in total food consumption in any condition, and in the choice environment, where lifespan extension was greatest, mutant flies consumed a sugar:protein ratio that was statistically indistinguishable from control animals (Figure 4B right two bar groups).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 4B comparing genotypes.

claim: In the choice environment, mutant flies consumed a sugar:protein ratio that was statistically indistinguishable from control animals.
source: More importantly, we found no differences among genotypes in total food consumption in any condition, and in the choice environment, where lifespan extension was greatest, mutant flies consumed a sugar:protein ratio that was statistically indistinguishable from control animals (Figure 4B right two bar groups).
evidence: Supported by nutrient-specific food intake measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutant flies show the same extent of increased sugar consumption as control animals in the choice environment.
source: First, mutant flies show the same extent of increased sugar consumption as control animals in the choice environment (Figure 4B, third bar group).
evidence: Supported by sugar consumption measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The lifespans of Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies are reduced to a similar extent as control animals when the carbohydrate content of a fixed diet is increased.
source: Second, the lifespans of Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies are reduced to a similar extent as control animals when the carbohydrate content of a fixed diet is increased (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D), showing that their lifespan is equally or more sensitive to dietary carbohydrate.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data on high sugar diets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Gross metabolites including total protein, fat, and carbohydrate abundances are strongly increased in the choice environment, and mutant and control animals are similarly affected.
source: Third, gross metabolites that are known to be influenced by food intake, including total protein, fat, and carbohydrate abundances (Lee et al., 2008; Skorupa et al., 2008), are strongly increased in the choice environment, and mutant and control animals are similarly affected (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5, with citations to previous work on metabolite-diet relationships.

claim: Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies are eating the same amount of the same food, and they are processing nutrients similarly to control animals, in both the fixed- and choice-diet regimes.
source: It appears, therefore, that Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies are eating the same amount of the same food, and they are processing nutrients similarly to control animals, in both the fixed- and choice-diet regimes.
evidence: Inferred from the combined food intake and metabolite data presented in Figures 4B and 5.

claim: The macronutrient valuation process itself is a potent factor that modulates organismal aging independent of food consumption.
source: Based on the roles of serotonin and 5HT2a in the valuation of dietary protein, we propose that the macronutrient valuation process itself is a potent factor that modulates organismal aging independent of food consumption.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the combined findings that mutants have extended lifespan in choice conditions despite equivalent food intake and nutrient processing.

claim: Mutation in JhI-21 abolished protein preference in starved flies.
source: Interestingly, we found that mutation in JhI-21 abolished protein preference in starved flies (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from JhI-21 mutants shown in Figure 6A and supplementary figures.

claim: JhI-21 mutant animals failed to increase neuronal serotonin after 3 hr of yeast feeding, establishing that it is required for protein-dependent serotonin production.
source: We also discovered evidence that JhI-21 acts upstream of serotonin signaling; JhI-21 mutant animals failed to increase neuronal serotonin after 3 hr of yeast feeding, establishing that it is required for protein-dependent serotonin production (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by serotonin measurements in JhI-21 mutants shown in Figure 6B.

claim: JhI-21 mutant females exhibited a normal increase in egg production with dietary protein concentration.
source: JhI-21 mutant females exhibited a normal increase in egg production with dietary protein concentration (Figure 6C), and they showed normal feeding in both fixed and choice environments (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by egg laying assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: JhI-21 mutant flies showed normal feeding in both fixed and choice environments.
source: JhI-21 mutant females exhibited a normal increase in egg production with dietary protein concentration (Figure 6C), and they showed normal feeding in both fixed and choice environments (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mutation in JhI-21 resulted in a modest (13%) increase in mean lifespan in a fixed-diet condition.
source: Nevertheless, mutation in JhI-21 recapitulated the extended lifespan pattern observed in Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies with a modest (13%) increase in mean lifespan in a fixed-diet condition (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) and a greater (32%) mean lifespan extension in a choice-diet environment (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data on fixed diet shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mutation in JhI-21 resulted in a greater (32%) mean lifespan extension in a choice-diet environment.
source: Nevertheless, mutation in JhI-21 recapitulated the extended lifespan pattern observed in Trh and 5HT2a mutant flies with a modest (13%) increase in mean lifespan in a fixed-diet condition (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) and a greater (32%) mean lifespan extension in a choice-diet environment (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data on choice diet shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The JhI-21 amino acid transporter and possibly SLC7 protein family members in general are conserved regulators of protein-dependent behavior and physiology.
source: These data suggest that the JhI-21 amino acid transporter, and possibly SLC7 protein family members in general, are conserved regulators of protein-dependent behavior and physiology and that they may function together with serotonin signaling to modulate aging independently of mechanisms that regulate reproduction and total food intake.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the JhI-21 mutant phenotypes and its homology to SLC7A5.

claim: JhI-21 may function together with serotonin signaling to modulate aging independently of mechanisms that regulate reproduction and total food intake.
source: These data suggest that the JhI-21 amino acid transporter, and possibly SLC7 protein family members in general, are conserved regulators of protein-dependent behavior and physiology and that they may function together with serotonin signaling to modulate aging independently of mechanisms that regulate reproduction and total food intake.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the combined findings that JhI-21 mutants show extended lifespan without changes in reproduction or food intake.

claim: Protein restriction extends lifespan in crickets, flies, mice, and probably humans.
source: Protein restriction extends lifespan in crickets (Reddiex et al., 2013), flies (Mair et al., 2005), mice (Solon-Biet et al., 2014), and probably humans (Levine et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in multiple species.

claim: Many of the effects of diet manifest independently of food consumption, likely through global integration of nutrient signals and cell non-autonomous responses to those signals directed by the nervous systems.
source: Remarkably, however, many of the effects of diet manifest independently of food consumption, likely through global integration of nutrient signals and cell non-autonomous responses to those signals directed by the nervous systems (Linford et al., 2011; Mair et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work demonstrating diet effects independent of consumption.

claim: Sensory neurons in Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans can promote or limit lifespan depending on the specific neurons involved.
source: Indeed, sensory neurons in Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans can promote or limit lifespan depending on the specific neurons involved (Alcedo and Kenyon, 2004; Apfeld and Kenyon, 1999; Libert et al., 2007), and the first instance of sensory modulation of lifespan in mice was recently reported (Riera et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on sensory modulation of lifespan.

claim: Tryptophan hydroxylase (Trh) is a rate-limiting enzyme for neuronal serotonin synthesis and is the Drosophila homologue of TPH2.
source: Flies with significantly reduced tryptophan hydroxylase (Trh), a rate-limiting enzyme for neuronal serotonin synthesis (Neckameyer et al., 2007) that is the Drosophila homologue of TPH2, exhibited a reduction in preference for both autolyzed yeast and BSA compared with control animals (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work characterizing Trh function.

claim: In Drosophila, there are five known serotonin receptors, each of which is evolutionarily conserved: 5HT1a, 5HT1b, 5HT2a, 5HT2b, and 5HT7.
source: In Drosophila, there are five known serotonin receptors, each of which is evolutionarily conserved: 5HT1a, 5HT1b, 5HT2a, 5HT2b, and 5HT7 (D. E. Nichols and C. D. Nichols, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work cataloging Drosophila serotonin receptors.

claim: Ketanserin is a serotonin receptor 2a (5HT2a) antagonist.
source: Silencing of serotonergic neurons and treatment of flies with a serotonin receptor 2a (5HT2a) antagonist, ketanserin (Colas et al., 1995), eliminated preference entirely, such that starved animals exhibited an aversion to dietary protein that mimicked what we routinely observed from fully-fed, control animals.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work characterizing ketanserin.

claim: A BLAST analysis comparing vertebrate SLC7A5 to the fly protein database revealed the gene juvenile hormone inducible 21 (JhI-21) as the most likely homolog.
source: A BLAST analysis comparing vertebrate SLC7A5 to the fly protein database revealed the gene juvenile hormone inducible 21 (JhI-21) as the most likely homolog (see also, Piyankarage et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by BLAST analysis and citation to previous work.

claim: In mice, a lysosomal amino acid transporter has been shown to communicate luminal amino acid levels to the canonical cellular amino acid sensor, TOR.
source: In mice, a lysosomal amino acid transporter has been shown to communicate luminal amino acid levels to the canonical cellular amino acid sensor, TOR (Attardo et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work in mice.

claim: In Drosophila, an insect glycine transporter, Slimfast, together with certain solute carrier 6 family members are critical for organismal growth.
source: In Drosophila, an insect glycine transporter, Slimfast, together with certain solute carrier 6 family members are critical for organismal growth (Colombani et al., 2003; Goberdhan et al., 2005), and several orphan Drosophila amino acid transporters in adipocytes regulate ovarian stem cell number (Armstrong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on amino acid transporters in Drosophila.

claim: Several orphan Drosophila amino acid transporters in adipocytes regulate ovarian stem cell number.
source: In Drosophila, an insect glycine transporter, Slimfast, together with certain solute carrier 6 family members are critical for organismal growth (Colombani et al., 2003; Goberdhan et al., 2005), and several orphan Drosophila amino acid transporters in adipocytes regulate ovarian stem cell number (Armstrong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Trh is found in 83 neurons per hemisphere of the brain based on immunostaining of adult Drosophila.
source: Based on immunostaining of adult Drosophila, Trh is found in 83 neurons per hemisphere of the brain (Bao et al., 2010), and 5HT2a is concentrated in small groups of glomeruli such as the ellipsoid body, large field R-neurons, antennal lobe, and a subset of gustatory neurons in the suboesophageal ganglion (Nichols, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous immunostaining work.

claim: 5HT2a is concentrated in small groups of glomeruli such as the ellipsoid body, large field R-neurons, antennal lobe, and a subset of gustatory neurons in the suboesophageal ganglion.
source: Based on immunostaining of adult Drosophila, Trh is found in 83 neurons per hemisphere of the brain (Bao et al., 2010), and 5HT2a is concentrated in small groups of glomeruli such as the ellipsoid body, large field R-neurons, antennal lobe, and a subset of gustatory neurons in the suboesophageal ganglion (Nichols, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on 5HT2a localization.

claim: Serotonin is acting acutely during the post-ingestive phase to drive behavioral and health outcomes.
source: Moreover, by combining temporal neuronal manipulations with continuous feeding measures we were able to provide, for the first time, evidence that serotonin is acting acutely during the post-ingestive phase to drive behavioral and health outcomes.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal manipulation experiments showing serotonin is required during choice phase but not starvation phase.

claim: Specific genetic and environmental manipulations, such as dietary restriction, insulin signaling and mate availability rapidly and reversibly affect mortality rates, often within hours or days.
source: This is consistent with reports showing that specific genetic and environmental manipulations, such as dietary restriction (Good and Tatar, 2001; Mair et al., 2003; Smith et al., 2008), insulin signaling (Giannakou et al., 2007) and mate availability (Gendron et al., 2014; Maures et al., 2014) rapidly and reversibly affect mortality rates, often within hours or days.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work demonstrating rapid effects on mortality.

claim: The same neural circuits that evaluate internal and external nutritional status to determine what and when to eat also interact with major hormone axes known to influence aging, such as insulin-like and TGFβ signaling.
source: It is also notable that the same neural circuits that evaluate internal and external nutritional status to determine what and when to eat also interact with major hormone axes known to influence aging, such as insulin-like and TGFβ signaling (Domingos et al., 2011; You et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on neural circuit interactions with hormone signaling.
